intro: This unit opens two real pages of the Babylonian Talmud and reads them closely. The first is Berakhot 2a–3a, the Talmud's opening page, about when to say the evening Shema. The second is from tractate Shabbat: the stories of Hillel and three visitors on 31a, and the rules for Hanukkah lights on 21b.

You will read each passage in translation, with Rodkinson's public-domain English (1896–1903) as one tool and modern translations in paraphrase as another. You will follow the moves of the argument: question, proof, objection and answer. You will also ask what each ruling protects, such as a tired family, a curious stranger, or a household in danger.

By the end you will be able to cite a passage by tractate and page, name who is speaking, and explain how different readers have understood it. You will describe what the text says and how Jews have read it, without deciding what anyone should believe.
bigQuestion: How do close readings of real Talmud pages show argument and mercy working together?

title: Reading Real Passages: Berakhot and Shabbat

chapters.title: Berakhot 2a–3a: The Evening Shema
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the Talmud turn one short question about the evening prayer into a whole way of reading?

story.title: Where Does the Teacher Stand?
story.kicker: The Talmud's very first question is not about the answer. It is about where the question came from.
paragraphs: A student opens a printed volume of the Babylonian Talmud to its first page. The page number is not 1. It is 2a, because printers counted the title page as page one. In the center sits a short block of Hebrew. That block is the Mishnah, a law code edited around the year 200 CE. Its first line asks a practical question: from what time may a person say the Shema in the evening?

The Shema is a prayer built from verses in Deuteronomy. Rabbinic tradition holds that it is said twice a day, at night and in the morning. The Mishnah gives three answers about the evening time. Rabbi Eliezer says one thing. The Sages say another. Rabban Gamliel says a third. No one is silenced, and all three views stay on the page.

Then the Gemara begins. The Gemara is the long discussion that later teachers built around the Mishnah. Its first words do not ask which answer is right. They ask something stranger: where does the tanna stand? A tanna is a teacher of the Mishnah. The Gemara wants to know what the teacher already assumed when he asked "from what time."

That small question opens the whole book. It says that every rule rests on something earlier, and that a reader should dig for it. Students have started their Talmud study on this page for centuries. In this chapter you will read it closely, move by move, in translation.
story.think: Why might a book of law begin by asking where a question comes from instead of giving a rule?

lessons.title: A Tractate Called Blessings
lessons.mainIdea: Berakhot, meaning "blessings," is the first tractate of the Talmud, and it opens with the evening Shema.
reading: The Babylonian Talmud is arranged in six orders, and each order holds several tractates. A tractate is one book of the Mishnah and its Gemara. The very first tractate is called *Berakhot*, which means "blessings." It deals with prayers and blessings: the Shema, the standing prayer, and blessings said over food.

Berakhot opens with the *Shema*. The prayer takes its name from its first Hebrew word, "hear," in Deuteronomy 6:4. Rabbinic tradition holds that Jews recite it every evening and every morning. That practice comes from how the rabbis read Deuteronomy 6:7, which speaks of words said "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Why start the whole Talmud with the evening prayer and not the morning? The Gemara itself raises that question a little later on the page, as you will see. For now, notice the choice. The Talmud's first topic is a daily practice that ordinary people did at home. Law in this book begins with something close to everyday life.

words.d: one book of the Mishnah or Talmud, on one main subject
"blessings"; the first tractate of the Talmud, about prayers and blessings
a prayer made of verses from Deuteronomy, beginning "Hear, O Israel"; rabbinic tradition has it said evening and morning

look.title: A Daily Practice
look.text: Picture a home in Babylonia around 400 CE. The sun has set. A father finishes work and a child finishes chores. Before bed, both say the Shema. The rabbis ask: from what moment does "lying down" time begin?
look.prompt: Why might a book of law begin with a question that every household faced each night?

check.q: What does the name Berakhot mean?
check.why: Berakhot means "blessings"; the tractate deals with prayers and blessings.

check.q: Which prayer does the Talmud's first line discuss?
check.why: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 asks when the evening Shema may be said.

check.q: Which verse do the rabbis read as the source for saying the Shema at night and in the morning?
check.why: Deuteronomy 6:7 speaks of "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

lessons.title: Three Answers, All Kept
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 gives three different end times for the evening Shema and keeps every opinion.
reading: The Mishnah's first line reads, in paraphrase: from what time may one recite the Shema in the evening? From the hour when the priests go in to eat their *terumah*. Terumah was the gift of food that Israelites gave to priests. The Mishnah uses the priests' mealtime as a clock for the start of night.

Then come three end times. Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until the dawn rises. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Gamliel were leading teachers of the late first and early second centuries CE. "The Sages" means the majority of the teachers.

Notice what the Mishnah does. It does not name a winner in this line. It lists the voices side by side. Later Jewish law generally follows the Sages' midnight as the ideal, while treating dawn as the outer limit after the fact. Keeping the losing views is a habit you will see on almost every page. The Talmud treats a minority opinion as worth remembering.

words.d: the first written collection of rabbinic law, edited c. 200 CE
a food gift that Israelites gave to priests; priests could eat it only when ritually pure
in the Mishnah, the majority of the teachers, as opposed to one named rabbi

look.title: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1
look.text: From when may one read the Shema in the evening? From the hour the priests go in to eat their terumah, until the end of the first watch, says Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages say: until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: until dawn comes up.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 (Berakhot 2a), paraphrased from the Hebrew; compare Rodkinson's translation (1896–1903)
look.prompt: Which of the three opinions gives a person the most time? Why might a teacher want to keep all three?

check.q: In Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, what marks the start of the time for the evening Shema?
choices: When the priests go in to eat their terumah
check.why: The Mishnah uses the priests' evening meal of terumah as the marker of nightfall.

check.q: Which teacher says the evening Shema may be said until dawn?
check.why: Rabban Gamliel gives the latest limit, the rising of dawn.

check.q: What does the Mishnah do with the three different opinions?
choices: It crosses out the minority views
It lists them side by side and keeps them all
It picks Rabbi Eliezer as the only law
It says none of them matter
check.why: The Mishnah records all three voices, a habit the Talmud keeps throughout.

lessons.title: The Sons Come Home Late
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah tells how Rabban Gamliel's sons came home after midnight and he let them say the Shema, showing mercy inside the law.
reading: Right after the three opinions, the Mishnah tells a short story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home from a wedding feast after midnight. They told their father they had not yet said the Shema. The Sages had set midnight as the limit. Had the sons missed their chance?

Rabban Gamliel answered, in paraphrase: if dawn has not yet risen, you are still obligated to say it. Then the Mishnah explains the Sages' own view. When they said "until midnight," they meant it as a fence. A fence is a safety rule. It keeps a person far from breaking the real limit, so no one lazily waits until morning.

The story shows the course's second thread, mercy. The young men were not scolded for going to a wedding. They were given a way to keep the practice. It also shows the first thread, argument. The Mishnah does not just state a limit. It explains why a stricter limit was set. A reader learns both the rule and the reasoning that protects it.

words.d: in rabbinic law, an extra safeguard set around a rule so people do not come close to breaking it
required to do something by law
a celebration meal after a wedding; in the Mishnah, the reason the sons came home late

look.title: A Late Night
look.text: It is 1 a.m. Two brothers walk home from a friend's wedding. They remember the Shema. One says, "Too late, the Sages said midnight." The other says, "Let's ask Father."
look.prompt: Using Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, what would Rabban Gamliel say, and how does the idea of a fence explain his answer?

check.q: Why did Rabban Gamliel's sons come home late?
choices: They were at a wedding feast
check.why: The Mishnah says they came back from a wedding feast.

check.q: What does the Mishnah say the Sages meant by "until midnight"?
choices: It was the exact moment the law ends
It was a mistake they later took back
It was a fence to keep people far from the real limit
check.why: The Mishnah explains the Sages set midnight as a safeguard, while the true limit was dawn.

check.q: Which course thread does Rabban Gamliel's answer to his sons show most clearly?
choices: Mercy: he finds a way for them to keep the practice
A ruling that weddings are forbidden
check.why: He tells them they may still say the Shema before dawn, a merciful reading of the law.

lessons.title: The Gemara's First Question
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara opens by asking what earlier source the Mishnah's teacher assumed when he asked "from what time."
reading: The Gemara on Berakhot 2a begins with a short Aramaic question, often quoted as "tanna heikha kai?" It means "where does the *tanna* stand?" A tanna is a teacher from the time of the Mishnah. The question points at a hidden assumption. The Mishnah asks "from what time" as if everyone already knows there is a duty to say the Shema at night.

So where did that duty come from? The Gemara wants the root. This is a key move in almost every *sugya*. A sugya is one unit of Talmudic discussion on a topic. It often begins by asking for the source of a rule, the reason behind it, or the assumption it hides.

Readers across Jewish life notice this opening. Traditional yeshiva students learn to ask "where does the tanna stand?" as a habit. Academic scholars read it as a sign of how the editors of the Talmud worked: they tie each rule back to Scripture or to an earlier teaching. Both kinds of readers agree that the Gemara prizes questions.

words.d: the discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis, mostly in Aramaic, edited c. 500–600 CE
a teacher from the time of the Mishnah (to c. 200 CE)
one unit of Talmudic discussion on a single topic

look.title: Find the Hidden Assumption
look.text: Imagine a school rule that says, "From what time may students enter the library at lunch?" Before answering, a student asks, "Wait, where does it say students may use the library at lunch at all?"
look.prompt: How is this student's question like the Gemara's first question on Berakhot 2a?

check.q: What does the Gemara's first question, "where does the tanna stand?", ask?
choices: Where the teacher's house was located
What earlier source or assumption the Mishnah's teacher relied on
Whether the tanna was standing or sitting
Which city the Mishnah was written in
check.why: The question asks for the root of the duty the Mishnah takes for granted.

check.q: What is a sugya?
choices: One unit of Talmudic discussion on a topic
check.why: A sugya is a single discussion in the Gemara, with its questions and answers.

check.q: In what language is most of the Gemara written?
check.why: The Gemara is mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, while the Mishnah is in Hebrew.

lessons.title: Two Roots for One Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara offers two sources for the evening Shema: the verse about lying down, and the creation story's "evening and morning."
reading: The Gemara gives a first answer: the tanna stands on the verse. Deuteronomy 6:7 says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The rabbis read lying down as nighttime and rising up as morning. The duty exists because the verse says so, and the Mishnah just asks when it starts.

Then the Gemara adds a second possibility. Maybe the tanna learned it from the story of creation. Genesis 1:5 says, "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Evening comes first in the verse. So, the Gemara suggests, the Mishnah teaches the evening Shema first too.

This answers a question you met earlier. Why does the Talmud start with the evening and not the morning? The creation verse gives a reason: in the Hebrew Bible the day begins at evening. This is why Jewish holidays and Shabbat begin at sundown. Two proofs, one from law and one from creation, support the same rule.

words.d: in the Gemara, a verse or earlier teaching brought to support a claim
one numbered line of a biblical book, such as Deuteronomy 6:7
the first book of the Hebrew Bible, which tells of creation

look.title: The Verse Behind the Rule
look.text: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 6:7, The Holy Scriptures According to the Masoretic Text (Jewish Publication Society, 1917)
look.prompt: Which words in this verse do the rabbis read as "night" and "morning"?

check.q: Which verse does the Gemara use to explain why the Mishnah starts with evening?
choices: Genesis 1:5, "there was evening and there was morning"
check.why: Genesis 1:5 names evening before morning, so the Mishnah can begin with evening.

check.q: How do the rabbis read "when thou liest down" in Deuteronomy 6:7?
choices: As a rule about beds in the Temple
As the time for the nighttime Shema
As a command to rest on Shabbat
check.why: The rabbis link lying down with night and rising up with morning.

check.q: Why do Jewish holidays and Shabbat begin at sundown, according to this reading?
choices: Because the priests could not see in daylight
Because the Mishnah forgot the morning
Because in Genesis 1 evening comes before morning
check.why: The creation account lists evening first, and rabbinic tradition counts the day from evening.

lessons.title: Priests and Stars
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara reads the priests' mealtime as a sign of nightfall, the time when the stars come out.
reading: Why does the Mishnah use priests eating terumah as its clock? The Gemara explains through a verse in Leviticus 22:7. A priest who became ritually impure had to immerse in water. Then, in the verse, when the sun is down he is clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy food.

So the priests went in to eat their terumah once night had truly come. The Gemara connects that moment with the appearance of the stars. Later Jewish practice still uses the phrase *tzeit ha-kokhavim*, "the coming out of the stars," to mark nightfall. Many Jewish calendars print this time each day.

Here the Gemara reads the Mishnah's words as a code. The Mishnah could have said "when the stars come out." Instead it named a practice from the Temple, which had been destroyed in 70 CE by the time the Mishnah was edited. Some readers say this kept the memory of the Temple alive in daily prayer. Others see it simply as a well-known sign of night.

words.d: in biblical law, a status that kept a person from holy food or places until purified
"the coming out of the stars"; the rabbinic marker of nightfall
to go fully under water to become ritually pure

look.title: A Clock Without a Clock
look.text: There are no wristwatches in the ancient world. You need a sign that everyone can see or know. One teacher names the priests' dinner. Another might name the first three stars in the sky.
look.prompt: What makes a good public sign of nightfall? Why might the Mishnah choose one tied to the Temple?

check.q: According to the Gemara's reading of Leviticus 22:7, when could a purified priest eat terumah?
choices: At noon on the next day
check.why: The verse says once the sun is down he is clean and may eat holy food.

check.q: What does tzeit ha-kokhavim mean?
choices: The coming out of the stars
The first watch of the night
check.why: It is the rabbinic phrase for nightfall, marked by visible stars.

check.q: By the time the Mishnah was edited, what had happened to the Temple in Jerusalem?
choices: It had been destroyed in 70 CE
It was being run by the Sages
check.why: The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, over a century before the Mishnah (c. 200 CE).

lessons.title: The Poor Man's Dinner
lessons.mainIdea: A teaching quoted in the Gemara marks nightfall by when a poor person sits down to bread and salt.
reading: The Gemara on Berakhot 2b brings a *baraita*. A baraita is a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it. This baraita offers a different sign for the start of the evening Shema. It says: from the time a poor person comes in to eat bread with salt.

The Gemara then compares this sign with the priests' sign. Are they the same moment or not? The Gemara tests one against the other, asking which comes earlier. It even brings a third opinion about when people sit down to their Friday night meal. The discussion goes back and forth, and not every question is neatly closed.

Readers notice who is used as the clock here. First it was priests, the most honored class. Now it is the poor, who worked until dark and ate the simplest meal. Some teachers point out that the Talmud puts the poor worker's evening on the same page as the priest's. The rule about prayer quietly records how ordinary people lived.

words.d: a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was left out of the Mishnah itself
a challenge in the Gemara that shows a problem with a claim
the simple meal of a poor laborer in the Talmud's world

look.title: Two Clocks for One Night
look.text: Clock A: when the priests go in to eat holy food. Clock B: when a poor worker comes home to eat bread and salt. The Gemara asks whether these two clocks show the same time.
look.prompt: Why might the time differ for priests and for a poor worker? What does it show that both are on the page?

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A teaching from the Mishnah's era that is not in the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is an outside tannaitic teaching the Gemara quotes.

check.q: What sign of nightfall does the baraita on Berakhot 2b give?
choices: When a poor person comes in to eat bread with salt
check.why: The baraita uses the poor man's simple evening meal as its marker.

check.q: What does the Gemara do with the priests' sign and the poor man's sign?
choices: It compares them to see whether they match
It ignores the poor man's sign
check.why: The Gemara tests one teaching against another, a typical move in a sugya.

lessons.title: Three Watches or Four?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara records a disagreement over whether the night has three watches or four, and gives signs for each.
reading: The Mishnah's Rabbi Eliezer said "until the end of the first watch." So the Gemara on Berakhot 3a asks: how many watches does the night have? A watch is a shift of the night, like a guard's turn. Rabbi Eliezer holds there are three. Rabbi Natan, another tanna, holds there are four.

The Gemara adds signs for each watch in Rabbi Eliezer's view. In the first watch, a donkey brays. In the second, dogs bark. In the third, a baby nurses at its mother's breast and a wife talks with her husband. These are sounds anyone in an ancient village would know. The Gemara also records an *aggadah* there: at each watch God roars like a lion, grieving over the Temple.

Here law and story sit side by side. A question about timing leads to a picture of a whole village at night, and to a teaching about sorrow for the destroyed Temple. Readers have long found this mix typical of the Talmud. The book moves easily from a legal detail to a scene of grief and back.

words.d: one part of the night, like a guard's shift
the story and teaching parts of the Talmud, as opposed to law
a tanna who, in Berakhot 3a, holds the night has four watches

look.title: Dividing a Twelve-Hour Night
look.cite: Berakhot 3a, as discussed by the Gemara; rounded to equal hours
look.prompt: If Rabbi Eliezer's first watch ends after four of twelve hours, how much of the night does his view leave for the evening Shema?

check.q: How many watches does Rabbi Eliezer say the night has, in Berakhot 3a?
check.why: Rabbi Eliezer counts three watches; Rabbi Natan counts four.

check.q: Which sign does the Gemara give for the second watch?
check.why: In the Gemara's list, dogs bark in the second watch.

check.q: What is aggadah?
choices: The legal rulings of the Talmud
A list of the night watches
The story and teaching parts of the Talmud
check.why: Aggadah is the Talmud's narrative and ethical material; halakhah is its law.

lessons.title: David's Harp at Midnight
lessons.mainIdea: On Berakhot 3b the Gemara tells that a harp over King David's bed played at midnight and woke him to study, linked to Psalm 119:62.
reading: A little further on, the Gemara turns to midnight. It quotes a verse from Psalms, which tradition credits to King David: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto Thee." How did David know the exact moment of midnight? The Gemara on Berakhot 3b answers with a story.

A harp hung above David's bed. When midnight came, a north wind blew through its strings and it played by itself. David would rise and study Torah until dawn. The story is aggadah. It is a picture of a king who set aside part of every night for learning.

Readers take this story in different ways. Some traditional readers hold it as a true account of David. Many modern and academic readers treat it as a teaching image about devotion and study. Rashi, the great commentator from France (1040–1105), explains details of the scene. All these readers agree the story ties the question of time to a love of learning.

words.d: a book of the Hebrew Bible made of songs and prayers; tradition credits many to King David
the middle of the night; in the Mishnah, the Sages' limit for the evening Shema
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of France, the best-known commentator on the Talmud

look.title: A Verse About Midnight
look.text: At midnight I rise to give thanks to You, because of Your righteous rulings.
look.cite: Psalm 119:62, paraphrased; cited in Berakhot 3b. Compare the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: How does the Gemara use this verse to connect midnight, David and study?

check.q: What made David's harp play at midnight, in the Gemara's story?
choices: A north wind blowing through its strings
check.why: Berakhot 3b says a north wind blew on the harp at midnight.

check.q: What did David do after the harp woke him, in the story?
check.why: The story pictures David rising to study through the rest of the night.

check.q: How do many modern academic readers treat the harp story?
choices: As a law about buying harps
As a proof that the Shema is said at noon
As a teaching image about devotion and study
As a mistake by the printers
check.why: Readers differ: some take it as history, many read it as an aggadic image.

lessons.title: Rodkinson Against the Page
lessons.mainIdea: Michael Rodkinson's English Talmud (1896–1903) is public domain and readable, but it is partial and abridged, so readers check it against the page.
reading: Most students first meet the Talmud in translation. One of the earliest English versions was made by Michael L. Rodkinson and published in New York from 1896 to 1903. Because it is old, it is now in the public domain. That means anyone may copy and share it freely. It is easy to find online.

Rodkinson's version has real strengths. It was one of the first attempts to put Talmud tractates into plain English for general readers. But scholars point out its gaps. It is partial, since it covers only some tractates. It is abridged, since Rodkinson shortened and rearranged passages. Its quality is uneven from volume to volume.

So a careful reader compares. Put Rodkinson's lines next to the Hebrew and Aramaic page, or next to a modern translation such as the Steinsaltz or Schottenstein editions or the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria. Those modern versions are not public domain, so they are cited and paraphrased. Ask: did the translator skip a step of the argument? Checking translations is part of reading closely.

words.d: no longer under copyright; free for anyone to copy and share
shortened, with parts left out
a text carried from one language into another

look.title: English Talmud Translations Over Time
look.cite: Publication dates as commonly given for the Rodkinson (New York) and Soncino (London) translations
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the end of Rodkinson and the start of Soncino? Why might a newer, fuller translation have been wanted?

check.q: Why may students freely quote Rodkinson's translation?
choices: It was written by the Mishnah's editors
It is the only translation that exists
It was printed in the Vilna Shas
It is in the public domain
check.why: Rodkinson's work (1896–1903) is old enough to be out of copyright.

check.q: Which is a known weakness of Rodkinson's translation?
choices: It is abridged and covers only part of the Talmud
It is written only in Aramaic
It was banned in the United States
check.why: Scholars note it is partial, shortened and uneven.

check.q: Why must the Soncino and Sefaria's William Davidson translations be paraphrased here?
choices: They are too old to read
They are not in the public domain
check.why: Both are still under copyright or restrictive licenses, so this course paraphrases them.

lessons.title: Mapping the Moves
lessons.mainIdea: Reading Berakhot 2a as a map of moves — question, proof, second proof, test — shows how a sugya works.
reading: Now put the pieces together as a map. First comes the Mishnah: a question and three opinions. Next the Gemara asks for the root: where does the tanna stand? Then come two proofs, one from Deuteronomy 6:7 and one from Genesis 1:5. After that the Gemara tests signs of nightfall, the priests and the poor man, against each other.

Each step has a name students can learn. A *kushya* is a hard question or objection. A *terutz* is an answer that resolves it. "Mai ta'ama?" means "what is the reason?" When the Gemara cannot settle a point, it may say *teyku*, "let it stand." Learning these names helps you see the shape under the words.

Many Jewish students learn these moves with a *chavruta*, a study partner. Partners read aloud, argue, and push each other to explain. Orthodox yeshivas, Conservative and Reform schools, and university classes all use partner study in different ways. The goal is the same: to follow the argument and to see what each step protects.

words.d: a hard question or objection in the Gemara
an answer that resolves an objection
a study partner, or the practice of studying Talmud in pairs
"let it stand"; the Gemara's word when a question stays unresolved

look.title: Label the Steps
look.text: 1) The Mishnah asks when the evening Shema begins. 2) The Gemara asks what the teacher assumed. 3) It answers with Deuteronomy 6:7. 4) It offers Genesis 1:5 instead. 5) It compares the priests' sign with the poor man's sign.
look.prompt: Label each step as question, proof or test. Which step would you call the turning point?

check.why: A kushya is the Gemara's objection; a terutz answers it.

check.q: What does teyku mean?

check.why: Teyku marks a question the Gemara leaves unresolved.

check.q: What is a chavruta?
choices: A study partner, or studying in pairs
check.why: Chavruta study pairs learners who read and argue together.

chapters.title: Shabbat 31a and 21b: Hillel's Convert and the Hanukkah Lights
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the stories of Hillel's patience and the rules for Hanukkah lights show about how the Talmud joins law and kindness?

story.title: The Bet of Four Hundred Zuz
story.kicker: Two men bet money on whether anyone could make Hillel lose his temper.
paragraphs: The Talmud tells this story on Shabbat 30b–31a. Two men made a bet. Whoever could make Hillel angry would win four hundred zuz. A zuz was a silver coin, so this was a large sum. Hillel was a famous teacher who lived around the end of the first century BCE. The Talmud remembers him for his patience.

It was Friday afternoon, just before Shabbat. Hillel was washing his hair. One man came to his door and shouted, "Is Hillel here?" Hillel wrapped himself and came out. "My son, what do you need?" The man asked a silly question about why people from one land have round heads. Hillel treated it as a real question and gave a calm answer.

The man came back again, and then a third time, each time with another odd question about people from far places. Each time Hillel came out, called him "my son," and answered with care. At last the man burst out that Hillel had cost him four hundred zuz.

Hillel replied, in paraphrase: better that you lose four hundred zuz, and four hundred more, than that Hillel should lose his temper. The Gemara then tells three more stories of people who came to Hillel and to his colleague Shammai. In this chapter you will read those stories, and then a page about Hanukkah, from the same tractate.
story.think: The man's questions were meant to annoy. Why do you think Hillel answered them as if they were real questions?

lessons.title: Hillel and Shammai
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel and Shammai were leading teachers of the late first century BCE, and the Talmud often sets Hillel's patience beside Shammai's strictness.
reading: Hillel and Shammai are two of the most famous names in the Talmud. They lived in the land of Israel around the end of the first century BCE and the start of the first century CE. Rabbinic tradition lists them as the last of the "pairs" of leaders in Mishnah Avot. Hillel had come from Babylonia, and tradition says he was poor in his youth.

Each founded a school of students. The schools are called Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai. The Talmud records hundreds of their disputes. In most cases Jewish law follows the House of Hillel. The Talmud on Eruvin 13b explains why: the students of Hillel were gentle and humble, and they taught Shammai's view before their own.

The stories on Shabbat 31a use these two men as contrasts. Shammai is shown as strict and quick to send people away. Hillel is shown as patient and welcoming. Readers note that the Talmud still keeps Shammai's opinions and calls him a sage. The contrast is about how to teach, not about who was a good person.

words.d: a leading sage (late 1st century BCE) known in the Talmud for patience and gentleness
Hillel's colleague, known in the Talmud for strict rulings
"the House of Hillel"; the school of Hillel's students

look.title: Two Teachers
look.text: A new student comes to class late with a hard question. Teacher A says, "Not now, come back when you are ready." Teacher B says, "Sit down, let's start with what you know."
look.prompt: Which teacher is more like Shammai in these stories, and which is more like Hillel? Could both have good reasons?

check.q: About when did Hillel and Shammai live?
choices: Around the end of the first century BCE
check.why: Both are dated to the late first century BCE and early first century CE.

check.q: In most disputes, which house does Jewish law follow?
check.why: The Talmud (Eruvin 13b) says the law generally follows Beit Hillel.

check.q: According to Eruvin 13b, why did the House of Hillel's view usually become the law?
choices: It won a vote held in Babylon
Its students were gentle and taught Shammai's view first
check.why: The Talmud credits Hillel's students' humility and fairness.

lessons.title: On One Foot
lessons.mainIdea: A man asked to learn the whole Torah on one foot; Shammai sent him away, and Hillel answered with a single rule of kindness.
reading: On Shabbat 31a a man who was not Jewish came to Shammai. He said he would convert if Shammai taught him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring rod in his hand. The man then went to Hillel with the same request.

Hillel accepted him and said, in paraphrase: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah. The rest is its explanation. Now go and learn it. Hillel's saying is close to the *golden rule*, but it is phrased in the negative: do not do what you would hate.

Readers have taken this answer in several ways. Many stress the first half, a short summary of ethics. Many also stress the last words, "go and learn." Hillel did not say the rest was unimportant. He gave a starting point and sent the man to study. Reform, Conservative and Orthodox teachers all quote this passage, often with different emphasis.

words.d: a person who joins a religion not born into; here, one who wished to become Jewish
the teaching to treat others as you would want to be treated
an explanation of a text; Hillel calls the rest of the Torah the explanation of his rule

look.title: Hillel's Answer
look.text: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is explanation. Go and learn.
look.cite: Shabbat 31a, paraphrased; compare Rodkinson, Tract Sabbath (1896–1903) and the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Which part of Hillel's answer do you think matters most, the rule or "go and learn"? Explain.

check.q: What did the man ask Shammai to do?
choices: Teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot
Build him a house in one day
Light the Hanukkah lamp for him
check.why: On Shabbat 31a he asked to learn the whole Torah on one foot.

check.q: What did Shammai hold when he pushed the man away?
check.why: The Talmud says Shammai used the builder's rod in his hand.

check.q: How is Hillel's rule different from the usual golden rule wording?
choices: It is phrased as what not to do
check.why: Hillel says do not do to others what is hateful to you.

lessons.title: Only the Written Torah
lessons.mainIdea: A second visitor accepted only the Written Torah, and Hillel showed him through the alphabet that reading itself depends on teachers.
reading: The second visitor asked Shammai how many Torahs Jews have. Shammai said two: the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. The man said he trusted the written one but not the oral one. He wanted to convert on that condition. Shammai sent him away. Rabbinic tradition holds that the Oral Torah is the teaching passed down beside the written text.

Hillel accepted him and began to teach him the Hebrew alphabet: aleph, bet, gimel, dalet. The next day Hillel taught him the letters in a different order. The man objected that yesterday it was different. Hillel answered, in paraphrase: you had to rely on me for the letters. Rely on me for the oral teaching too.

The story makes a point about reading. Even letters need a teacher to explain them. Rabbinic tradition used this to defend the Oral Torah. Groups that accept only the written Bible, such as the Karaites who arose in the eighth and ninth centuries CE, have read it differently. This course describes these views without judging which is true.

words.d: the Five Books of Moses as a written text
in rabbinic tradition, teaching passed on by word of mouth alongside the Written Torah, later recorded in the Mishnah and Talmud
Jews who accept the written Bible but not rabbinic oral law as binding

look.title: Who Taught You the Letters?
look.text: Think back to learning to read. Someone pointed at a shape and said, "This is A." You trusted them. Later you read whole books on your own.
look.prompt: How does Hillel use the alphabet to make his point? Is his argument strong? Explain from the story.

check.q: What did the second visitor refuse to accept?
check.why: He accepted only the Written Torah, not the oral teaching.

check.q: How did Hillel teach the second visitor?
choices: He taught the alphabet in one order, then another
He told him to stand on one foot
He gave him four hundred zuz
check.why: Hillel changed the order of the letters to show reliance on a teacher.

check.q: Which later group accepted the written Bible but not rabbinic oral law?
check.why: The Karaites, from the 8th–9th centuries CE, reject rabbinic oral law as binding.

lessons.title: The Man Who Wanted to Be High Priest
lessons.mainIdea: A third visitor wanted to become High Priest; Hillel let him study until he discovered the limit himself, and all three later praised Hillel's patience.
reading: The third visitor passed a synagogue and heard the High Priest's fine clothes being described. He went to Shammai and asked to convert so he could become High Priest. Shammai pushed him away too. Hillel accepted him, and said, in paraphrase: does anyone become a king without learning the ways of the kingdom? Go and study.

The man studied. He reached a verse in Numbers 1:51, which warns that an outsider who comes near the holy service shall be put to death. He asked whom it meant. Hillel said it included even King David. The man reasoned that if even David could not serve, then surely a newcomer could not. He accepted this, and he stayed.

Later the three converts met. The Talmud gives their words, in paraphrase: Shammai's impatience nearly drove us from the world. Hillel's patience brought us under the wings of the Divine Presence. The passage ends by praising patience in teaching. It shows *mercy* as a way of teaching: let a learner reach the answer at their own pace.

words.d: the chief priest who led the Temple service in Jerusalem
in rabbinic writing, the Shekhinah, God's presence as described among people
kindness and patience shown to someone, especially a person who might be turned away

look.title: What the Three Converts Said
look.text: Shammai's short temper almost pushed us out of the world. Hillel's patience brought us close, under the wings of the Divine Presence.
look.cite: Shabbat 31a, paraphrased; compare Rodkinson, Tract Sabbath (1896–1903)
look.prompt: Why does the Talmud let the converts, not the rabbis, have the last word?

check.q: Why did the third visitor want to convert?
choices: He wanted to study on one foot
He wanted to win a bet
He wanted to become High Priest
He wanted to light Hanukkah lamps
check.why: He heard the High Priest's clothes described and wished to wear them.

check.q: How did the third visitor learn he could not be High Priest?
choices: He studied Numbers 1:51 and reasoned it out himself
check.why: Hillel let him study until he reached the verse and drew the conclusion.

check.q: What did the three converts say brought them close?
check.why: They credited Hillel's patience for bringing them under the wings of the Divine Presence.

lessons.title: The Question on 21b
lessons.mainIdea: On Shabbat 21b the Gemara stops a discussion of lamp oils to ask, "What is Hanukkah?"
reading: Tractate *Shabbat* is about the laws of the day of rest. Its second chapter begins with which oils and wicks may be used for the Shabbat lamp. That talk of lamps leads to Hanukkah lights. On Shabbat 21b the Gemara asks a plain question: "What is Hanukkah?"

The Mishnah itself says almost nothing about Hanukkah. There is no Mishnah tractate for it. So the Gemara answers with a baraita. It says that from the 25th of the month of Kislev there are eight days of Hanukkah. On them people do not give mourning speeches or fast.

Historians connect Hanukkah with the Maccabees, a Jewish family that led a revolt against the Seleucid Greek king Antiochus IV. They rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem around 164 BCE. The books of Maccabees tell that history. The Talmud's own answer, as you will see, focuses on a different detail: the oil.

words.d: the weekly day of rest; also the name of the tractate about its laws
an eight-day festival from 25 Kislev, marking the Temple's rededication
a month in the Hebrew calendar, usually in November or December
the Jewish family that led a revolt against Seleucid rule in the 160s BCE

look.title: Hanukkah by the Numbers
look.cite: Shabbat 21b; historians' common dating of the rededication, c. 164 BCE
look.prompt: The Mishnah has no tractate on Hanukkah. What might that tell you about where the Gemara had to look for its answer?

check.q: Where does the question "What is Hanukkah?" appear?
check.why: The Gemara asks it on Shabbat 21b, in a discussion of lamps.

check.q: On what date does Hanukkah begin, according to the baraita?
check.why: The baraita says eight days of Hanukkah begin on 25 Kislev.

check.q: Why does the Gemara use a baraita to explain Hanukkah?
choices: The Mishnah has no tractate on Hanukkah
check.why: With little in the Mishnah, the Gemara draws on an outside tannaitic teaching.

lessons.title: The Cruse of Oil
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara's answer tells of one sealed jar of oil that lasted eight days, and of the holiday set the next year.
reading: The baraita on Shabbat 21b continues. When the Greeks entered the Temple, they made all its oils impure. When the Hasmonean family won, they searched and found one *cruse* of oil. A cruse is a small jar. It still had the High Priest's seal, so it was pure.

The jar held enough oil to light the Temple lamp for only one day. The Talmud says a miracle happened, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year, it says, the sages set these days as a festival for praise and thanksgiving. Praise here means Hallel, a set of psalms sung on holidays.

Readers compare this account with the books of Maccabees, which tell of the battles and the rededication but not the oil. Some traditional readers accept both accounts. Some historians suggest the rabbis stressed the oil to focus on God's help rather than on war. This course reports those readings without deciding among them.

words.d: a small jar for oil
the priestly family of the Maccabees, who later ruled Judea
psalms of praise (Psalms 113–118) sung on festivals

look.title: The Sealed Jar
look.text: When the Hasmoneans prevailed, they searched and found only one jar of oil sealed by the High Priest. It had enough for one day. A miracle was done, and they lit from it eight days. The next year these were made days of praise and thanks.
look.cite: Shabbat 21b, paraphrased from the baraita; compare Rodkinson, Tract Sabbath (1896–1903)
look.prompt: What detail proves the oil was pure in the story? Why would that matter?

check.q: How did the Hasmoneans know the jar of oil was pure?
choices: It still had the High Priest's seal
It was brand new from Babylon
It was found under the altar
check.why: The baraita says the jar was sealed with the High Priest's seal.

check.q: How many days did the oil last, in the Talmud's account?
check.why: There was oil for one day, and it burned for eight.

check.q: What do the books of Maccabees focus on, compared with Shabbat 21b?
choices: The battles and rededication, not the oil
check.why: The books of Maccabees tell the military history; the Talmud stresses the oil.

lessons.title: The Lamp at the Door
lessons.mainIdea: The Hanukkah lamp is placed at the door facing the street, to make the miracle public, but inside on a table in time of danger.
reading: The Gemara on Shabbat 21b also gives rules for where to put the lamp. It says, in paraphrase, that it is a *mitzvah* to place the Hanukkah lamp at the entrance of one's house, on the outside. The purpose is to publicize the miracle, so people passing by can see it.

There are exceptions. A person who lives upstairs may place it at a window facing the street. And in a time of danger, the Gemara says, it is enough to set it on one's table inside. The rabbis knew that in some times and places a public religious sign could put a family at risk.

The rule shows both threads of the course. The law is careful: where, when and why. And it bends to protect life. Across Jewish communities today, some light at the doorway, some at a window, and many at a table. Chicago families, like families in many cities, often set their lamps in a front window facing the street.

words.d: a commandment; in common use, also a good deed
in rabbinic law, the reason the Hanukkah lamp is shown to passersby
a situation where following a practice openly could bring harm

look.title: Door, Window or Table?
look.text: Family A lives in a house on a quiet street. Family B lives on the fourth floor. Family C lives in a town where showing a religious sign in public is unsafe.
look.prompt: Using Shabbat 21b, where might each family place its Hanukkah lamp? What does the rule protect in each case?

check.q: Where does the Gemara say to place the Hanukkah lamp in the usual case?
choices: On the roof of the synagogue
At the entrance of the house, on the outside
check.why: Shabbat 21b says to place it outside at the door.

check.q: What is the reason given for placing the lamp where passersby can see it?
choices: To show the time of night
check.why: The goal is that the miracle be seen and remembered.

check.q: What does the Gemara allow in a time of danger?
choices: Placing the lamp on a table inside
check.why: In danger, it is enough to set it on the table, which protects the family.

lessons.title: Up or Down?
lessons.mainIdea: The House of Shammai lights eight lights on the first night and one fewer each night; the House of Hillel starts with one and adds one.
reading: The Gemara on Shabbat 21b lists levels of the practice. The basic mitzvah is one light for each household each night. Those who beautify the practice light one for each person in the house. For those who beautify it most, the Houses of Shammai and Hillel disagree.

The House of Shammai says: on the first night light eight lights, and then one fewer each night. The House of Hillel says: on the first night light one, and then one more each night. Both agree there are eight nights. They differ in direction, down or up.

Jewish practice today follows the House of Hillel. That is why most Hanukkah lamps grow brighter as the week goes on. But the Talmud keeps Shammai's view. A student reading the page sees a real argument with two sides, not only the answer that later won.

words.d: "the House of Shammai"; the school of Shammai's students
doing a commandment in a more generous or lovely way than required
a disagreement between teachers, recorded in the Talmud

look.title: Lights on Each Night
look.cite: Shabbat 21b, the Houses of Shammai and Hillel
look.prompt: On which night do the two Houses come closest? What does the chart show about the two directions?

check.q: How many lights does the House of Shammai light on the first night?
check.why: Beit Shammai starts with eight and goes down one each night.

check.q: Which house does Jewish practice follow today for Hanukkah lights?
choices: Neither; the lights are not lit
check.why: Most families follow Beit Hillel, adding one light each night.

check.q: What is the basic mitzvah of Hanukkah lights in Shabbat 21b?
choices: One light per household each night
Eight lights per person on night one
One light for the whole city
A light only on the last night
check.why: The baseline is one light for the household; more is beautifying the practice.

lessons.title: The Reasons Behind the Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara gives reasons for each house: days still to come or already gone, the Sukkot bulls, and "raise holiness, do not lower it."
reading: The Gemara asks: what is the reason? Two amoraim in the land of Israel, it says, gave explanations. An *amora* is a teacher of the Gemara period. One explanation: Shammai counts the days still to come, so the number goes down. Hillel counts the days already gone, so the number goes up.

The other explanation links Shammai to the bulls offered on Sukkot. Numbers 29 lists thirteen bulls on the first day and one fewer each day after. Hillel's reason is a principle: in matters of holiness, we go up and do not go down. A holy practice should grow, not shrink.

The page shows how the Gemara works. It does not just record who said what. It asks for reasons and offers more than one. Readers often note that Hillel's rule, "go up in holiness," says something beyond Hanukkah. It asks a person to keep growing. Shammai's reasons, based on counting and Temple offerings, are kept alongside it.

words.d: a teacher of the Gemara period (c. 200–500 CE)
the autumn festival of booths; Numbers 29 lists its Temple offerings
a general rule that explains many cases

look.title: Two Ways to Count
look.text: A countdown: 8, 7, 6 … 1. A count up: 1, 2, 3 … 8. One tracks what is left. One tracks what has been done.
look.prompt: Which way of counting matches the House of Shammai and which the House of Hillel? Which reason do you find stronger, and why?

check.q: What is an amora?
choices: A teacher of the Mishnah period
A teacher of the Gemara period
check.why: Amoraim taught after the Mishnah; tannaim taught before c. 200 CE.

check.q: What principle supports the House of Hillel?
choices: Count the days that are left
In holiness, go up and do not go down
check.why: Hillel's reason is to increase in holiness.

check.q: Which offering does one reason link to the House of Shammai?
check.why: The Sukkot bulls decrease each day, as Shammai's lights do.

lessons.title: Halakhah Beside Aggadah
lessons.mainIdea: Shabbat 21b and 31a mix law and story on the same pages, and each helps explain the other.
reading: The Talmud has two kinds of material. *Halakhah* is law: how, when and where to act. Aggadah is story and teaching: the lives of the sages, legends and sayings. In Shabbat 21b, the history of the oil (aggadah) sits right beside the rules for the lamp (halakhah).

The Hillel stories on 31a are aggadah too. Yet they teach something about law. Hillel's answer to the first convert sums up the Torah as a rule for how to treat others. The patience stories show how a teacher should apply the law to a person who stands before him.

Rabbinic readers have long debated how the two fit. Some say aggadah gives the reason behind halakhah. Some treat aggadah more freely, as teaching rather than law. Most agree the Talmud meant them to be read together. You cannot fully understand the lamp rule without the oil story, or Hillel's law without his patience.

words.d: Jewish law, the rules for how to act, as the Talmud develops it
the story, legend and ethical teaching in the Talmud
a traditional story passed down about the past

look.title: Sort the Passage
look.text: A) Eight days of Hanukkah begin on 25 Kislev. B) One jar of oil burned for eight days. C) Place the lamp at the door. D) Hillel came out to answer a rude question.
look.prompt: Sort each line as halakhah or aggadah. Then explain how one story line helps a law line make sense.

check.q: Which line from Shabbat 21b is halakhah?
choices: Place the Hanukkah lamp at the door of the house
One jar of oil burned for eight days
check.why: The lamp's placement is a rule for action, so it is halakhah.

check.q: Which describes aggadah?
choices: Stories, legends and ethical teachings in the Talmud
The page numbers of the Talmud
check.why: Aggadah is the Talmud's narrative and moral material.

check.q: How do most readers say halakhah and aggadah should be read?
choices: Together, each helping explain the other
check.why: Readers widely agree the Talmud presents them side by side on purpose.

lessons.title: Two Translations Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Setting Rodkinson's older English beside a modern paraphrase shows what translators add, cut and change.
reading: Rodkinson's translation of tractate Shabbat is one of the older public-domain English versions. His style is formal, with a nineteenth-century sound. He also shortened and rearranged some passages. So when you read the Hillel stories or the Hanukkah page in his version, check each step against a modern translation or the Hebrew and Aramaic page.

Modern translations such as the Steinsaltz edition, the Schottenstein edition and the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria add explanations inside the text, often in a different type. That helps new readers follow the argument. But it also means the reader sees the translator's choices mixed in with the Talmud's words.

No translation is the page itself. A good habit is to ask three things. What words did the translator choose? What did the translator add to explain? What did the translator leave out? Readers from yeshivas, from university classrooms and from synagogue study groups all use this habit in their own ways.

words.d: a person who carries a text from one language into another
a recent printing or translation of the Talmud, often with added explanation
a language of the ancient Near East; most of the Gemara is in it

look.title: Two Versions of One Line
look.text: Version 1 (older, formal style): a short line where Hillel tells the man that what he hates he should not do to his neighbor. Version 2 (modern, with added words): a longer line where the translator explains in brackets that "neighbor" means any fellow person.
look.prompt: What does Version 2 add? What might a reader gain or lose from that addition?

check.q: Why check Rodkinson's Shabbat against a modern translation or the page?
choices: He added the Hanukkah lights himself
He was the editor of the Mishnah
He shortened and rearranged some passages
check.why: Rodkinson's version is abridged and uneven, so checking is needed.

check.q: What do many modern Talmud translations add inside the text?
choices: Explanations to help readers follow the argument
New laws not in the Talmud
check.why: Editions like Steinsaltz and the William Davidson Talmud weave in explanation.

check.q: Which is a good question to ask of any translation?
choices: What did the translator leave out?
How many lamps does it light?
check.why: Asking what was added, chosen and left out is key to close reading.

review.q: What did Hillel say was "the whole Torah" to the man on one foot?
choices: Light one more lamp each night
What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow
review.why: Shabbat 31a gives Hillel's rule, followed by "go and learn."

review.q: How much money was bet on making Hillel angry?
review.why: The story on Shabbat 30b–31a names a bet of four hundred zuz.

review.q: How did Hillel show the second convert he needed the Oral Torah?
choices: By teaching him the alphabet in two orders
review.why: Hillel showed that even letters depend on a teacher.

review.q: What verse did the would-be High Priest study before changing his mind?
review.why: Numbers 1:51 warns an outsider not to come near the holy service.

review.q: In the Gemara's account, what made the one jar of oil usable?
choices: It had the High Priest's seal, so it was pure
It was bought for four hundred zuz
review.why: The seal showed the Greeks had not made it impure.

review.q: Which house starts with one light and adds one each night?
review.why: Beit Hillel increases; Beit Shammai decreases.

review.q: Why may the lamp be placed inside on a table?
choices: In a time of danger, to protect the family
review.why: Shabbat 21b allows the table in time of danger.

review.q: Which pair shows halakhah and aggadah together on Shabbat 21b?
choices: The lamp's placement and the story of the oil
The night watches and the poor man
review.why: The oil story and the lamp rules share one page.
